title: Scaling regimes of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation from the functional renormalization group
authors: Liubov Gosteva, Nicolás Wschebor, Léonie Canet
abstract: We revisit the renormalization group (RG) approach to the one-dimensional stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation and show that previous approaches based on perturbative Wilsonian RG with a sharp cutoff are not valid, even though they yield a qualitatively correct picture. The reason is that taking momentum derivatives while using the sharp cutoff is not well-defined in some cases and leads to intrinsic divergencies. This is a well-known problem of Wilsonian RG, which can be simply cured by using a smooth cutoff, and employing the functional renormalization group (FRG) framework. We establish the flow equations for the KS model within the FRG, and demonstrate that it flows to the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) fixed point at large scales. We then calculate the full two-point correlation function over a wide range of momenta and frequencies. We show that it exhibits three universal scaling regimes that we characterize: the KPZ regime (with dynamical exponent $z=3/2$), the Edwards-Wilkinson regime (with $z=2$) and the recently discovered inviscid regime (with $z=1$). The latter develops over an extended range of large wavenumbers and originates from the vanishing of the effective viscosity. Lastly, we investigate the large-scale behavior of the deterministic KS equation by studying the limit of vanishing noise and we determine the scales where the KPZ regime can emerge in the deterministic case.
summary: This work rigorously re-examines the scaling behavior of the stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation using the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG). By employing a smooth cutoff, the authors successfully identify three distinct universal scaling regimes: KPZ, Edwards-Wilkinson, and an inviscid regime. This provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding crossover dynamics in nonlinear physical systems.
main_problem: The study aims to correctly characterize the universal scaling regimes of the one-dimensional stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation by improving upon flawed Renormalization Group (RG) techniques.
main_result: The analysis establishes three distinct universal scaling regimes—KPZ ($z=3/2$), Edwards-Wilkinson ($z=2$), and an inviscid regime ($z=1$)—by employing the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG).
method: The core method is the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG) framework, which uses a smooth cutoff to derive flow equations for the effective average action, avoiding divergences encountered with sharp cutoffs.
model_or_system: The model analyzed is the stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, which describes dynamics in nonlinear field theories relevant to interface growth and pattern formation. It is compared against the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) universality class.
key_observables: The full two-point correlation function, characterized by its dynamical exponent $z$ across different momentum/frequency ranges.

main_assumptions: The use of the FRG framework with smooth regulators is crucial; previous perturbative Wilsonian RG approaches using sharp cutoffs are deemed invalid.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the fixed points of the 1D KPZ equation, showing stable IR (KPZ) and UV/intermediate regimes (EW, IB). Figure 6 shows the flow of expansion parameters in both standard and specialized p0-DE approximations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of FRG over older RG methods. It then derives the flow equations for the KS model within the FRG framework using various approximations (DE, NLO). Finally, it analyzes the resulting flow to identify and characterize the three distinct universal scaling regimes by calculating correlation functions.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of advanced non-perturbative field theory tools like FRG to nonlinear PDEs provides deep insights into universality classes in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, which is highly relevant for understanding complex dynamics in condensed matter systems.
